item.title: Kernel Operation and Privilege Control of Special Permissions (SetUID, SetGID, Sticky Bit) in Linux
item.description:
When multiple users share and operate on a single system resource in a Linux environment, standard permission structures (rwx for Owner/Group/Others) alone cannot achieve delegation of privileged operations or secure access control within directories. For example, when a regular user changes their own password, they need to update the /etc/shadow file, which normally only root has write permission to. To meet such operational requirements, the Linux kernel incorporates special permission bits (SetUID, SetGID, Sticky Bit) inside the 16-bit file mode structure (st_mode).

Structure of st_mode (16-bit Integer Mask)

In a file system, permission information is stored as the st_mode structure (16-bit integer) inside the inode. When an administrator executes a command like chmod 755, it is evaluated inside the kernel as four digits (0755), including the omitted leading octal digit.

+-------------------+----------------------+---------------------------------------+
| File Type Bitmask | Special Bits Bitmask | Standard Permission Bitmask (9 bits) |
| (4 bits) | (3 bits) | User (3b) | Group (3b) | Others (3b) |
+-------------------+----------------------+-----------+------------+--------------+
| Bit 15 - Bit 12 | Bit 11 - Bit 9 | Bit 8 - 6 | Bit 5 - 3 | Bit 2 - 0 |
+-------------------+----------------------+-----------+------------+--------------+

File Type Bitmask (Bit 15–12):

  • - : Regular File
  • d : Directory
  • c : Character Device
  • b : Block Device
  • s : Socket
  • l : Symbolic Link
  • p : Named Pipe (FIFO)
  • Special Permission Bitmask (Bit 11–9):
  • Bit 11 (04000) : SetUID
  • Bit 10 (02000) : SetGID
  • Bit 9 (01000) : Sticky Bit
  • Standard Permission Bitmask (Bit 8–0):
  • rwx bits assigned to Owner / Group / Others respectively

SetUID (Set User ID - Octal 4000)

When a binary executable with SetUID set is executed, the kernel escalates the process execution privileges (Effective User ID: EUID) to the owner ID of the file instead of the user who launched the command (Real User ID: RUID).

chmod 4755 executable_file
# or
chmod u+s executable_file

In the notation of ls -l output, it is displayed in the owner’s execute permission (x) position. If execute permission is granted, it is displayed as a lowercase s (-rwsr-xr-x); if execute permission is missing, it is displayed as an uppercase S (-rwSr-xr-x).

/usr/bin/passwd is a typical application of SetUID. Even when executed by a regular user, the EUID is temporarily changed to root while the process is running, enabling updates to the privileged file /etc/shadow.

SetGID (Set Group ID - Octal 2000)

SetGID operates on group ownership for files and directories.

  • Application to executables: Changes the Effective Group ID (EGID) of the process to the file’s owner group ID at execution time.
  • Application to directories: Forces all files and subdirectories newly created within the directory to inherit the owner group ID of the parent directory, rather than the primary group of the creator.
chmod 2775 shared_directory
# Or
chmod g+s shared_directory

It is widely used in configurations where write permissions for newly generated files are inherited by a specific service group (such as the mail group), as seen in the /var/mail directory (drwxrwsr-x).

Sticky Bit (Octal 1000)

The Sticky Bit (Restricted Deletion Flag) is a flag that restricts users from unintentionally (or maliciously) deleting or renaming files created by others in a shared directory where all users have write permissions (777).

chmod 1777 shared_tmp
# Or
chmod +t shared_tmp

In a directory with the Sticky Bit set, only users who fall under one of the following can delete or rename files:

  1. Owner of the file
  2. Owner of the parent directory
  3. Superuser (root)

The /tmp directory (drwxrwxrwt) is a prime example of this setting.

Kernel-Level Process Identifiers

When executing a process, the Linux kernel maintains the following identifiers for privilege verification:

  • PID (Process ID): Unique identifier of the process
  • RUID (Real User ID): Actual user ID that launched the process
  • EUID (Effective User ID): User ID referenced by the kernel for access permission determination during resource access
  • RGID (Real Group ID): Primary group ID of the user that launched the process
  • EGID (Effective Group ID): Group ID referenced by the kernel during access permission determination

SetUID / SetGID achieve privilege escalation by temporarily swapping these EUID / EGID values.

Troubleshooting

1. Disabling Privilege Escalation via the nosuid Mount Option

⚠️ If a Permission Denied error occurs at execution time despite the SetUID/SetGID flags (e.g., 4755) being correctly set on the file, the corresponding file system may be mounted with the nosuid option.

On a partition where nosuid is enabled, the kernel completely ignores SetUID and SetGID bits for safety reasons.

💡 Verification and resolution flow:

$ findmnt -n -o OPTIONS -T /path/to/binary
rw,nosuid,nodev,relatime

If nosuid is included in the output above, you need to allow exec,suid by modifying the /etc/fstab configuration or manually remounting.

sudo mount -o remount,suid /path/to/mountpoint

2. Display Issues with Uppercase S or T Flags

⚠️ When executing the ls -l command displays uppercase letters such as -rwSr-xr-x or drwxrwxr-T, special permissions (SetUID/SetGID/Sticky Bit) are set, but the corresponding execute permissions (x) are not granted. In this state, privileged execution and proper directory traversal will not function.

🛠️ Resolution steps (re-granting execute permission):

# Fix uppercase S in SetUID
chmod u+x /path/to/binary

# Fix uppercase T in Sticky Bit
chmod o+x /path/to/directory

Audit and Verification Command Logs

💡 Terminal execution examples for checking the configuration status of special permissions within the system.

$ ls -ld /usr/bin/passwd /var/mail /tmp
-rwsr-xr-x. 1 root root 68208 Jul 16 2022 /usr/bin/passwd
drwxrwsr-x. 2 root mail 4096 Aug 23 10:00 /var/mail
drwxrwxrwt. 15 root root 4096 Aug 23 10:00 /tmp

$ find /usr/bin /usr/sbin -perm -4000 -type f -ls
 68208 68 -rwsr-xr-x 1 root root 68208 Jul 16 2022 /usr/bin/passwd
140521 144 -rwsr-xr-x 1 root root 147280 Jan 18 2024 /usr/bin/sudo
210943 52 -rwsr-xr-x 1 root root 51832 Feb 4 2024 /usr/bin/chfn

$ find /var -perm -2000 -type d -ls
 10482 4 drwxrwsr-x 2 root mail 4096 Aug 23 10:00 /var/mail

$ findmnt -t ext4,xfs,tmpfs
TARGET SOURCE FSTYPE OPTIONS
/ /dev/sda1 xfs rw,relatime,attr2,inode64,logbufs=8,logbsize=32k,noquota
/tmp tmpfs tmpfs rw,nosuid,nodev,seclabel

Configuration Notes

  • 🛠️ Minimizing SetUID: Assigning SetUID to unnecessary binaries leads to local privilege escalation vulnerabilities. Perform system audits regularly by running find / -perm -4000.
  • 💡 Migration to Capabilities: On modern Linux systems, instead of SetUID which grants root privileges to the entire binary, using Linux Capabilities (setcap command) to grant only the minimum required privileges (e.g., CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE) is recommended.
  • ⚠️ Sticky Bit and Shared Directories: When sharing network file systems such as NFS, ensure that client-side mount settings and UID/GID mappings are configured accurately.
